ai.definition: Autonomous Delivery Robots are small self-driving vehicles designed to transport goods along sidewalks and within campuses for last-mile delivery tasks.
ai.howItWorks: These robots use a combination of cameras, lidar sensors, and detailed mapping data to navigate their environment. They can operate on pedestrian paths, cross streets, and handle parcel handoffs with the assistance of remote operators who are available as backups in case of issues.
ai.problemSolved: They address the inefficiencies and high costs associated with last-mile delivery by automating the process, reducing human intervention needed for navigation and parcel handling.
ai.manufacturing: The manufacturing involves assembling components such as wheels, sensors (cameras, lidar), computing units, and communication systems. The robots are built in a modular fashion to allow for easy updates and maintenance of hardware and software.
ai.buildProcess: Robots are typically assembled using off-the-shelf parts and custom-built enclosures. They undergo rigorous testing in controlled environments before deployment in real-world settings.
ai.costDrivers: Key cost drivers include the initial development and production costs, ongoing maintenance expenses for sensors and computing units, and operational costs such as power consumption and data transmission fees.
ai.lifecycleOutlook: The technology is currently in a trial phase with limited deployments focusing on campuses and neighborhoods. It is expected to expand to broader urban areas as regulatory frameworks are established and public acceptance grows.
ai.regulation: Current regulations vary widely by region, with some areas allowing for pilot programs while others have strict limitations or outright bans. Standardization of guidelines will be crucial for wider adoption.
ai.risks: Safety concerns related to pedestrian interactions, cybersecurity risks from remote control systems, and potential legal issues around liability in case of accidents are significant challenges that need addressing.
ai.profitability: Profitability is currently uncertain due to the high initial investment required for development and deployment. However, as scale increases and operational costs decrease, there is potential for profitability through reduced labor costs and increased efficiency in delivery operations.
ai.futureDevelopment: Future developments may include enhanced autonomy with less reliance on remote operators, integration of AI for better decision-making, and improvements in battery technology to extend operating ranges without recharging.

glossary.def: Light Detection and Ranging, a remote sensing technology that uses light in the form of a pulsed laser to measure ranges (variable distances) to the Earth.

subsystems.name: Chassis and drivetrain
subsystems.role: a small wheeled platform stable enough to carry a parcel over kerbs and uneven paving.

subsystems.name: Perception sensors
subsystems.role: sense pedestrians, cyclists, pets, kerbs, crossings and obstacles.

subsystems.name: Onboard autonomy
subsystems.role: drive the route without a human, at walking pace, and stop safely when confused.

subsystems.name: Remote supervision
subsystems.role: one human watches many robots and drives any that get stuck.

subsystems.name: Power and charging
subsystems.role: run a shift on a battery and return to a base to recharge.

subsystems.name: Handoff and order backend
subsystems.role: links the robot to a shop or app and lets the customer open it.

buildSteps.title: Map the operating area
buildSteps.detail: Sidewalks, crossings, kerb heights and gradients are surveyed and turned into a high-definition map, because pavement maps rarely exist in usable form.

buildSteps.title: Design the chassis
buildSteps.detail: The platform is sized to carry a small parcel, climb kerbs of roughly 10 cm, and stay upright on slopes and in rain.

buildSteps.title: Assemble the sensor suite
buildSteps.detail: Cameras, lidar and ultrasonics are mounted, sealed and calibrated so their measurements agree.

buildSteps.title: Train the autonomy software
buildSteps.detail: Engineers collect and label thousands of hours of footage, then test perception and planning in simulation before road trials.

buildSteps.title: Build the robots
buildSteps.detail: Units are assembled in low volumes, each tested on an indoor track for braking, steering and lid closure.

buildSteps.title: Run a controlled pilot
buildSteps.detail: A campus or neighbourhood is mapped, a remote-operations centre is staffed, and a small fleet runs short routes with heavy supervision.

buildSteps.title: Scale the fleet
buildSteps.detail: Route density rises, more robots share one operator, and the service integrates with delivery apps and shops.

buildSteps.title: Operate and maintain
buildSteps.detail: Robots run shifts at about walking pace, return to dock to charge, and are cleaned and repaired between shifts.

the hard problems are unpredictable pedestrians, dogs, roadworks and wet leaves.
they make a shift's worth of range affordable.
stuck robots need a fallback, and one operator must cover many robots to make the economics work.
rules vary from city to city and often cap fleet size or speed.

pathway.milestone: pilot fleets delivering food and groceries on campuses and in a few neighbourhoods
pathway.unlocks: real data on reliability, cost per delivery and pedestrian behaviour.

pathway.milestone: one remote operator supervising many robots, with denser routes and app integration
pathway.unlocks: a cost per delivery that competes with a human courier.

pathway.milestone: purpose-built lightweight robots that cross roads and last several years
pathway.unlocks: coverage of ordinary residential streets, not just campuses.

pathway.milestone: shared curb-side charging and regulated pavement access in many cities
pathway.unlocks: robots as routine local infrastructure alongside bikes and scooters.
